title: Smallest Missing Genetic Value in Each Subtree
statement:
A rooted tree has `n` nodes labelled `0` to `n - 1`, with node `0` as the root. The array `parents` describes it: `parents[i]` is the parent of node `i`, and `parents[0]` is `-1`. Each node `i` also carries a genetic value `nums[i]`, a positive integer; no two nodes share a value.

The subtree of a node consists of the node itself together with everything below it. For every node `i`, find the smallest positive integer that is not the value of any node in the subtree of `i`. Return these answers as an array of length `n`, where position `i` holds the answer for node `i`.
constraints: parents describes a valid tree rooted at 0
All values in nums are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

If a subtree does not contain the value `1`, its answer is `1`. Values are distinct, so exactly one node holds `1` (if any), and the only subtrees containing it are those of that node and its ancestors. Every other node simply gets `1`.

Along that path from the node holding `1` up to the root, each subtree contains the previous one, so its set of values only grows and its answer never decreases. One growing `seen` set and one `missing` counter that only moves forward cover the whole path. Collecting each subtree from scratch (the brute force) costs O(n²).

## Approach

1. Fill `answer` with `1` and build the `children` lists from `parents`.
2. Find `node`, the node whose value is `1`. If there is none, return `answer`.
3. While `node` is not `-1`, run a DFS from it with a `stack`, skipping nodes already `visited`, and add every new node's value to `seen`. The part below the previous path node was visited already, so it is skipped.
4. Raise `missing` while `seen` contains it, store it in `answer[node]`, and move `node` to its parent.

## Example 1, step by step

`parents = [-1,0,0,2]`, `nums = [1,2,3,4]`. The value `1` sits at node `0`, the root, so the path is just node `0`. The DFS from node `0` visits nodes `0, 2, 3, 1` and `seen = {1,3,4,2}`. `missing` climbs from `1` to `5`, so `answer[0] = 5`; then `node` becomes `-1`. Nodes `1`, `2` and `3` keep `1`, giving `[5,1,1,1]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each node is visited once overall, and `missing` only increases, to at most `n + 1`.
- Space: O(n) for the child lists, the `visited` flags, the `stack` and `seen`.

## Pitfalls

- Restarting the DFS or the `missing` counter at every ancestor makes it quadratic on a long chain.
- A label can be larger than its parent's label, so do not assume `parents[i] < i`.
- Use an explicit stack: a chain of 10^5 nodes overflows a recursive DFS.
- Forgetting the case where no node holds `1`: every answer is then `1`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `answer` | the result; `1` for every node off the path |
| `children` | child lists built from `parents` |
| `node` | the current node on the path from value `1` to the root |
| `seen` | values found in the current node's subtree |
| `visited` | nodes whose value is already in `seen` |
| `missing` | smallest positive integer not in `seen` |
| `stack`, `current` | the DFS stack and the node popped from it |

narration.3: Every node starts with answer 1; only ancestors of the node holding 1 can do better.

narration.5: Turn the parent array into child lists so the DFS can go downwards.

narration.9: No node holds 1, so 1 is missing from every subtree.

narration.19: Nodes below the previous path node were already collected; skip them.

narration.23: Record its value as present in this subtree.
narration.25: Push its children to explore them next.

narration.31: This is the smallest value missing from the current node's subtree.
